$comment: The interpolation findings both analyses give the five files of the test project in this folder, copied verbatim from the user's interpolationtests project: analyzeKotlin in editors/vscode/src/analyze.ts and Analyzer.analyzeKotlin in streamlord-analysis, each file on its own, with the const vals the workspace declares (constants) known, as the VS Code index and IntelliJ provide them. Only the interpolation codes are listed (kotlin-interpolation, unescaped-interpolation, unsafe-interpolation), and missing-id and top-level-text must not appear in any file. Offsets count UTF-16 code units; line is for the reader. What IntelliJ adds with types is in the plugin's own InspectionTest.

A_LanguageComment.kt.message: Kotlin writes $name into the HTML as it is. If it can hold text from outside, build the string with interpolate(...), which escapes it.
Kotlin writes ${applicant.email} into the HTML as it is. If it can hold text from outside, build the string with interpolate(...), which escapes it.
Kotlin writes $count into the HTML as it is. If it can hold text from outside, build the string with interpolate(...), which escapes it.

Kotlin writes ${buttonAttributes()} into the markup's own structure: a tag name, an attribute name or a list of attributes. Fine for one chosen in code; a value from outside decides the markup itself, and escaping cannot prevent that.

Kotlin interpolates $open here, as the whole Datastar expression. Meant as a server value, only a number or a boolean is safe there; meant as the signal $open, make the whole literal $$"""...""" (Kotlin 2.2+), or escape as ${'$'}open.
